catalog_quote: The major stress pattern in Ambai is penultimate. Major stress is penultimate. Secondary stress occurs two syllables before major stress. These two rules are illustrated in (1) below. (1) S --> 'S / __ S ++ S --> "S / __ S 'S Examples of this major and secondary stress pattern are presented in (2). We note that diphthongs, although seen as one syllable, attract stress. (2) /'ran.do/ 'banana' /'a.to/ 'arrow' /a.'ri.kan/ 'child' /bo.'to.ru/ 'three' /"pi.ran.'di.ma/ 'bitter' /"bi.o.'mi.nin/ 'yellow' /"re.an.'te.nan/ 'first' /"man.ku.'kei/ 'chicken' The major stress rule is not affected by the addition of most postclitics; i.e stress does not move when clitics are added. ... Question marker -re and the demonstratives, however, cause stress to shift. ... The major stress rule has two minor exceptions ... audit.reasoning: The record rests on the sole reference grammar of Ambai (Silzer 1983, 309-pp ANU PhD, open access), which we hold as PDF + two text layers; the deciding quotation, the secondary-stress rule, the diphthong-attracts-stress statement (basis of the weight-sensitive (tentative) / CVV-heavy, right-edge coding), the clitic facts, the listed-set exceptions and the word-domain quote are all present verbatim at the cited pages (thesis pp. 37-40 = PDF pp. 55-58), and p.38 was re-verified as a page image (confirming /\"bi.o.'mi.nin/ against the scanned's 'bi.a.'). Glottolog 5.1's full [amk] bibliography and a Semantic Scholar search show no later phonology, prosody or instrumental work on Ambai; later items are morphology MA theses, a 23-pp sketch, lexicostatistic comparisons and literacy/health readers. The weight-hedged coding faithfully reflects Silzer's own hedge (penultimate default, but a final diphthong syllable tak
